Definition: An asexual propagation method wherein adventitious roots are induced to form on an intact, aerial stem by wounding or girdling the bark and enclosing the zone in a moist rooting substrate (such as sphagnum moss), severing the rooted shoot only after a viable root system has developed.
Example Sentence: Nursery propagators frequently utilize air layering on mature litchi (Litchi chinensis) and Ficus elastica to obtain large, true-to-type planting stock that would otherwise root poorly from conventional stem cuttings.
Etymology: Compound term from Middle English 'air' (via Old French from Greek ἀήρ, 'aēr', atmosphere) and 'layering' (from Middle English 'leyere', an established shoot laid down for rooting, from Old English 'lecgan', to lay).
See Also: layering, adventitious roots, girdling, sphagnum moss, clonal propagation

Definition: The asexual formation and development of a viable seed without meiosis (apomeiosis) and without fertilization (parthenogenesis), producing progeny that are maternal genetic clones of the seed parent.
Example Sentence: Commercial citrus propagators utilize natural apomixis (nucellar polyembryony) in rootstocks such as Rangpur lime to produce vigorous, uniform, true-to-type rootstocks free of systemic viruses.
Etymology: Coined in 1908 by German botanist Hans Winkler from Greek ἀπό ('apo-', without/away from) and μῖξις ('mixis', mingling or sexual union).
See Also: parthenogenesis, apospory, diplospory, adventitious embryony, polyembryony, parthenocarpy

Definition: The living genetic resources of an organism—encompassing seeds, pollen, vegetative propagules, or tissue cultures—maintained and conserved for plant breeding, crop improvement, and biodiversity preservation.
Example Sentence: Plant breeders routinely screen wild apple accessions from the National Plant Germplasm System to identify and introgress novel fungal resistance genes into commercial cultivars.
Etymology: Coined in 1883 by German biologist August Weismann as 'Keimplasma' (from Latin 'germen', bud or sprout, and Greek πλάσμα, 'plasma', something formed or molded).
Synonyms: genetic resources, hereditary material, gene pool
See Also: gene bank, landrace, accession, cryopreservation, inbred lines

Definition: The horticultural technique of joining vascular tissues of two distinct plant parts—the scion and the rootstock—so that they unite physiologically and continue their systemic growth as a single composite organism.
Example Sentence: Orchardists routinely perform cleft grafting and whip-and-tongue grafting in early spring to top-work mature fruit trees with high-value commercial cultivars.
Etymology: From Middle English 'graff'/'graft', from Old French 'graffe' (grafting tool, stylus), derived via Latin 'graphium' from Ancient Greek γραφεῖον (grapheion, 'stylus' or 'writing implement', describing the pencil-like tapered shape of a prepared scion).
See Also: scion, rootstock, graft union, callus tissue, vascular cambium, graft incompatibility

Definition: A seed capable of surviving extreme desiccation down to low moisture contents (2–5% fresh weight basis) and long-term hermetic storage at sub-zero temperatures (e.g. -18°C) without loss of viability, adhering predictably to Roberts' viability equations.
Example Sentence: Horticultural germplasm repositories preserve thousands of orthodox tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) and onion (Allium cepa) accessions in sealed moisture-proof foil packets at -18°C for decades.
Etymology: From Greek ὀρθός ('orthos', correct/straight) and δόξα ('doxa', opinion/doctrine); formalized in seed biology by E.H. Roberts in 1973 to describe seeds that follow standard storage principles.
See Also: recalcitrant seed, intermediate seed, seed vigor, cryopreservation, Roberts viability equation

Definition: A specialized form of vegetative propagation in which a single scion bud attached to a small shield of bark and wood (shield bud) is inserted into a T-shaped incision cut through the bark to the active vascular cambium of a rootstock.
Example Sentence: In commercial stone-fruit nurseries, propagators conduct T-budding in mid-to-late summer when the rootstock bark is actively 'slipping', facilitating rapid insertion and union of the shield bud.
Etymology: Named directly after the shape of the vertical and horizontal cuts forming a 'T' in the rootstock bark; combined with 'budding' (from Middle English 'budde', of Germanic origin).
See Also: chip budding, rootstock, scion, vascular cambium, bark slipping

Definition: A genuine botanical seed developed from a fertilized ovule inside a flower, distinguished in horticultural production from vegetative propagules (such as potato seed tubers, garlic cloves, or onion sets) colloquially referred to as 'seed'.
Example Sentence: In tropical vegetable production, adopting True Potato Seed (TPS) drastically lowers transportation costs and prevents the transmission of tuber-borne viral pathogens compared to bulky seed tubers.
Etymology: Compound term from Middle English 'trewe' (genuine, faithful) and Old English 'sǣd' (seed, what is sown); used to contrast embryonated ovules with asexual vegetative propagules.
See Also: True Potato Seed (TPS), vegetative propagule, seed tuber, seed piece, apomixis

Definition: The acquisition or acceleration of a plant's competence to flower through prolonged exposure to cold temperatures, rendering the shoot apical meristem competent for floral transition.
Example Sentence: Winter wheat cultivars and biennial horticultural crops such as cabbage and carrots require a prolonged period of vernalization before they can transition from vegetative growth to reproductive bolting and flowering.
Etymology: Coined from Neo-Latin 'vernalizatio' (from Latin 'vernalis', of spring, from 'ver', spring), introduced as a translation of the Russian agricultural term 'yarovizatsiya' (from Slavic 'Yarilo', god of spring).
See Also: photoperiodism, chilling requirement, bolting, devernalization, flowering locus c

Definition: A seed that is highly sensitive to desiccation and chilling injury, failing to survive drying below a relatively high critical moisture content (typically 15–30%) or storage at sub-zero temperatures due to the lack of protective LEA proteins and active metabolic respiration.
Example Sentence: Because jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus) and mango (Mangifera indica) produce recalcitrant seeds that lose viability within weeks of extraction, breeders must maintain them in field gene banks or cryopreserve excised embryonic axes.
Etymology: From Latin 'recalcitrare' (to kick back or rebel, from 're-' back + 'calcitrare' to kick, from 'calx' heel); classified by E.H. Roberts (1973) because these seeds 'rebel' against conventional dry, cold gene bank storage.
See Also: orthodox seed, intermediate seed, embryonic axes, cryopreservation, LEA proteins, chilling injury
